games.title: Colossal Cave Adventure
games.note: Will Crowther based its map on Kentucky's Mammoth Cave, which he had explored; Don Woods expanded it in 1977.

games.title: Zork
games.note: Its name was MIT slang for an unfinished program. Infocom later sold it in three parts as Zork I, II and III.

games.title: Adventureland
games.note: Fit into 16K of memory on a TRS-80, making it one of the first commercial adventure games for home computers.

games.title: Mystery House
games.note: Often called the first graphical adventure game. Its murder plot borrows from Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None.

games.title: King's Quest
games.note: IBM asked Sierra for it to show off the PCjr. Sir Graham could walk behind objects in each scene.

games.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
games.note: Douglas Adams co-wrote it with Infocom's Steve Meretzky, based on his own novel.

games.title: Colossal Cave (2023)
games.note: Ken and Roberta Williams came out of retirement to rebuild the original cave in 3D.

games.title: Astron Belt
games.note: A laserdisc shooter that mixed film footage with game graphics; Sega showed it at a 1982 US trade show.

games.title: MUD
games.note: Written at the University of Essex. Trubshaw named it Multi-User Dungeon after the Dungeon version of Zork.

games.title: AberMUD
games.note: Named after Aberystwyth, where students wrote it. It inspired TinyMUD, LPMud and DikuMUD.

games.title: DikuMUD
games.note: Named after DIKU, the University of Copenhagen's computer science department, where five students wrote it.

games.title: EverQuest
games.note: Richard Bartle described it as basically a DikuMUD with a graphical client bolted on.

games.title: Rogue
games.dev: Michael Toy & Glenn Wichman (later Ken Arnold)
games.note: The roguelike genre, with random dungeons and permanent death, is named after it.

games.title: Hack
games.note: Started by high school students after they played Rogue. Its code later became NetHack.

games.title: NetHack
games.note: Named for the internet, which its volunteer developers used to work together. It is still updated.

games.title: Moria (1983)
games.note: Written at the University of Oklahoma. The goal is to reach the bottom of the Mines of Moria and kill the Balrog.

games.title: Angband
games.note: Two University of Warwick students built it by expanding UMoria in 1990.

games.title: Spelunker
games.note: Its cave explorer dies from very short falls, which became a running joke among Japanese players.

games.title: Spelunky
games.note: Derek Yu released the first version free for Windows in December 2008.

games.title: The Binding of Isaac
games.note: A dungeon shooter with Zelda-style rooms, random items and permanent death.

games.title: FTL: Faster Than Light
games.note: Funded on Kickstarter. You manage a starship's crew and systems in pausable real time.

games.title: Impossible Mission
games.note: Greets players with digitized speech: 'Another visitor. Stay a while... stay forever!'

games.title: Torneko's Great Adventure: Mystery Dungeon
games.note: A Dragon Quest spin-off starring the merchant Torneko. It began Chunsoft's long Mystery Dungeon series.

games.title: Maze War
games.dev: Steve Colley, Greg Thompson & Howard Palmer
games.note: High school students made it at NASA Ames. A later MIT version let players at different universities fight over ARPANET.

games.title: MIDI Maze
games.note: Up to 16 Atari ST computers could be linked through their MIDI ports for deathmatches.

links.took: Exploring a cave world by typing commands, collecting treasures and solving puzzles.
links.added: A parser that understood full sentences, dry humor and the Great Underground Empire.

src.t: Game Developer, The History of Zork

links.extra: Zork's four authors began it at MIT in May 1977 after playing Adventure.

links.took: Mechanics close to Crowther and Woods's adventure, in a much smaller world.
links.added: A version that fit in 16K on a TRS-80 and was sold in stores.
links.extra: Scott Adams first tried to port Colossal Cave itself to the TRS-80, then wrote his own game.

links.took: Text-adventure play, which Roberta Williams loved and wanted more of.
links.added: A drawing for every room and a murder mystery plot.

src.t: PCGamesN, Ken and Roberta Williams interview

links.took: Moving between linked areas, carrying items to solve problems, and dragons.
links.added: Joystick control and real-time graphics in place of typed commands.

src.t: Game Developer, Playing Catch Up: Adventure's Warren Robinett

links.extra: Warren Robinett played Colossal Cave at Stanford's AI lab and set out to make a graphical version.

links.took: Exploring a dungeon by text. Toy and Wichman wanted that with replay value.
links.added: A new random dungeon every game, and death that erases your character.

links.took: Adventure-game puzzles. Ron Gilbert loved the game in college but missed having visuals.
links.added: Graphics and a point-and-click verb menu, so no typing was needed.

src.t: Wikipedia: Maniac Mansion, citing Ron Gilbert, GDC postmortem, 2011

links.took: Exploring a fantasy world by typing text commands.
links.added: Many players sharing the same world at once over a network.

src.t: Wikipedia: Colossal Cave Adventure, citing PC Gamer and Game Developer, 2016

links.took: Adventure-game exploration, combined with Rogue's random dungeons.
links.added: A Tolkien quest down through the Mines of Moria to the Balrog.

links.took: Crowther and Woods's original cave, puzzles and treasures.
links.added: Full 3D graphics and VR, rebuilt by Ken and Roberta Williams.

src.t: Vice, on Roberta Williams remaking the game

links.took: Rick Dyer's adventure concept, which was inspired by the text game Adventure.
links.added: Don Bluth's film-quality animation on laserdisc, played by timing moves to the action.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon's Lair, citing a Rick Dyer interview, Animation World Network

links.took: Using a laserdisc for arcade graphics, which Dyer saw at the 1982 AMOA show.
links.added: Hand-drawn cartoon animation instead of filmed footage, with the player guiding a knight.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon's Lair, citing Wolf, The Video Game Explosion

links.took: Its name. Trubshaw called it Multi-User Dungeon after Zork's Dungeon version.
links.added: A shared online world where many players met, fought and teamed up.
links.extra: Bartle stresses that MUD was a big departure from Zork, not a multiplayer copy.

links.took: Infocom's Zork-born parser and game engine.
links.added: Douglas Adams's jokes and puzzles that tease and mislead the player.

links.took: Roberta Williams's graphic adventure design, at the company Mystery House launched.
links.added: Animated color scenes where Sir Graham walks around, made for the IBM PCjr.

links.took: Graphic adventures. Gilbert saw King's Quest over Christmas and liked its pictures.
links.added: No typing: a verb menu and cursor, and a cast of playable teens.

src.t: Wikipedia: Maniac Mansion, citing Ron Gilbert, GDC postmortem, 2011

links.took: Ron Gilbert's SCUMM engine and point-and-click verb interface.
links.added: Pirate comedy, insult swordfighting and a design that avoids sudden deaths.

links.took: MUD1's gameplay, which Alan Cox had played at Essex.
links.added: A version written at Aberystwyth that spread to other universities.

links.took: Its combat-focused online dungeon style. Diku's authors wanted a better AberMUD.
links.added: Classes, levels and code so easy to run that it spawned more worlds than any rival.

src.t: Wikipedia: DikuMUD, citing Richard Bartle and Raph Koster

links.took: Diku-style class-and-level group combat, as designers like Raph Koster note.
links.added: A 3D graphical world shared by thousands of players.
links.extra: Verant denied using Diku code. Richard Bartle called EverQuest a DikuMUD with a graphical client bolted on.

links.took: Diku-style classes, quests and group combat, per Raph Koster.
links.added: A polished, accessible world with gentler death penalties and easier grouping.

links.took: Online world gameplay. Lead designer Raph Koster said Diku inspired Ultima Online.
links.added: A graphical open world with player housing, crafting and player-killing.

links.took: The MMORPG template. Many Blizzard developers were EverQuest fans.
links.added: Easier grouping, gentler deaths and quests that spread players across zones.

links.took: Inspiration from Michael Toy's time playing the turn-based text game Star Trek.
links.added: A fantasy dungeon drawn in text characters and rebuilt randomly each game.

links.took: Rogue's random dungeons. Its authors wanted their own version.
links.added: Pets, shops and many more items and monsters.

links.took: Hack's code, which NetHack's developers took over and extended.
links.added: Development shared over the internet, adding roles, gods and deep item interactions.

links.took: Random dungeons and permanent death. Koeneke got hooked on Rogue at university.
links.added: A town with shops and a deep Tolkien dungeon ending with the Balrog.

src.t: Wikipedia: Moria (1983), citing Craddock, Dungeon Hacks, and Koeneke's Usenet history

links.took: UMoria's code, which two Warwick students expanded.
links.added: Many more items, monsters and features, set in Tolkien's Angband.

links.took: Its town-and-dungeon roguelike design, which shaped Diablo's first plans.
links.added: Real-time action, mouse control and online co-op.

src.t: Wikipedia: Moria (1983), citing Russ Pitts, The Escapist, 2006

links.took: Randomized levels and items. Brevik called Angband 'the model of what we wanted'.
links.added: Real-time clicking combat, a gothic town and online co-op on Battle.net.

src.t: Wikipedia: Angband, citing Ars Technica War Stories, 2020
PC Gamer, The moment the action-RPG was born

links.extra: Diablo was first planned as a turn-based roguelike before the team switched to real time.

links.took: Roguelike dungeon-crawl design, which David Brevik has acknowledged.
links.added: Real-time combat, mouse-driven play and online co-op.

src.t: Wikipedia: Roguelike, on David Brevik's influences

links.took: Roguelike design, which Brevik named among Diablo's influences.
links.added: Real-time action and simple controls that took the formula to a mass audience.

src.t: Wikipedia: Roguelike, on David Brevik's influences

links.took: Interactive objects. The pickaxe that digs through walls came from NetHack.
links.added: Platforming caves with physics, generated fresh on every run.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spelunky, citing Derek Yu and The Making of Spelunky

links.took: Cave-exploring visuals, character design and mechanics, as Derek Yu describes.
links.added: Random levels and permanent death borrowed from roguelikes.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spelunky, citing Derek Yu, Spelunky (Boss Fight Books), 2016

links.took: The feel and physics of running and jumping.
links.added: Caves full of traps, shops and items that change every run.
links.extra: Derek Yu named the Super Mario series in general as one of his biggest inspirations.

links.took: Procedural levels and permanent death, Rogue's core ideas.
links.added: Real-time platforming, making it an early example of a 'roguelite'.

links.took: A model for applying roguelike design to another genre, credited by Edmund McMillen.
links.added: Twin-stick shooting through Zelda-style rooms with hundreds of random items.

links.took: Roguelike structure outside the dungeon crawl, which FTL's developers credit.
links.added: Managing a starship's crew, power and systems in pausable real time.

links.took: Random layouts. Dennis Caswell named Rogue as the source for shuffled rooms.
links.added: Acrobatic platforming, robot guards and digitized speech on the Commodore 64.

src.t: Wikipedia: Impossible Mission, citing Retro Gamer, 2013, and Edge, 2006

links.took: Rogue's random dungeons and turn-based moves. Chunsoft aimed for an easier Rogue.
links.added: Dragon Quest characters and friendlier rules for console players.

src.t: Wikipedia: Roguelike, citing Chunsoft's Koichi Nakamura

links.took: Torneko the merchant, plus Dragon Quest monsters and items.
links.added: Random, turn-based dungeons in the style of Rogue.

links.took: First-person 3D maze shooting, which Maze first showed in 1973.
links.added: Texture-mapped walls and color graphics on an ordinary PC.
links.extra: Maze is often called the first FPS, but historians say id's games started the genre without direct inspiration from it.

links.took: Players hunting each other through a first-person maze.
links.added: Up to 16 linked Atari STs and round smiley-face players.

links.took: Round Pac-Man-like players in a maze, one of the 3D variants Pac-Man inspired.
links.added: First-person networked deathmatch across linked Atari STs.
